summary: This bill requires federal agencies to prepare and publish analyses of whether proposed rules would raise average annual household costs by $50 or more before issuing them, and bars final rules that do so unless required by statute or needed for national security threats or presidentially declared disasters.

scores.thoughts: The bill establishes new procedural requirements for federal agencies when issuing rules that could affect household costs. It does not authorize, appropriate, or alter any government spending programs or budgets.
Taxes are listed as one component of household costs in the bill's definitions, but the legislation does not change tax rates, create new taxes, or modify tax policy in any way.
Healthcare costs are included in the definition of household costs, but the bill imposes no substantive changes to healthcare policy, coverage, or markets.
The bill contains no provisions related to firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, border policy, visas, or related enforcement.
The bill does not mention or affect abortion access, reproductive healthcare policy, or related regulations.
No provisions alter military or defense spending, procurement, or policy.

The bill creates a general barrier to rules that raise household costs by $50+/year and allows judicial review. Many environmental regulations affect energy and other costs, so the measure could indirectly constrain such rules, but the text does not target environmental policy specifically.
The legislation does not modify welfare programs, eligibility, or benefits.
Education-related costs appear in the household-cost definition, but the bill makes no changes to education funding, policy, or structure.
No references to drug enforcement, decriminalization, or related regulations.
The bill contains no provisions on sentencing, policing, or criminal justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
The bill does not alter fiscal policy, deficits, or debt management.
No provisions relate to LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
The legislation does not address foreign aid appropriations or policy.
No provisions concern voting access, election integrity, or electoral procedures.
The bill does not regulate technology companies, data privacy, or digital oversight.
Labor-related costs are mentioned in the household-cost definition, but the bill does not change labor law, union rights, or workplace regulations.
No provisions address religious exemptions, civil rights enforcement, or anti-discrimination policy.
